title: Influenza (Flu)
subtitle: A highly contagious respiratory illness caused by Influenza A, B, or C viruses that infects the nose, throat, and lungs.

sections.title: Symptoms
sections.intro: Flu symptoms come on suddenly and are more severe than the common cold. They typically appear 1, 4 days after exposure and last 5, 7 days.
items: Sudden high fever (38, 41°C) with chills
Severe muscle aches and body pains
Persistent dry cough and sore throat
Extreme fatigue and weakness
Headache, runny or stuffy nose
Vomiting and diarrhea (more common in children)

sections.title: Causes
sections.intro: Influenza viruses are RNA viruses belonging to the Orthomyxoviridae family. They mutate rapidly, which is why a new flu vaccine is needed every year.
items: Influenza A, most common, causes seasonal epidemics and pandemics
Influenza B, seasonal outbreaks, less severe than A
Influenza C, mild illness, not responsible for epidemics
H1N1, H3N2, common circulating subtypes of Influenza A

sections.title: Prevention
sections.intro: Annual flu vaccination is the single most effective way to prevent influenza. The vaccine is updated each year to match circulating strains.
items: Get the annual flu vaccine every autumn
Wash hands frequently with soap and water
Avoid close contact with sick people
Cover mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing
Stay home when sick to prevent spreading
Disinfect commonly touched surfaces

sections.title: Treatment
sections.intro: Most flu cases resolve on their own with rest and fluids. Antiviral medications can reduce severity if started within 48 hours of symptoms.
items: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Oseltamivir (Tamiflu), antiviral for high risk patients
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and pain
Avoid aspirin in children (risk of Reye's syndrome)
Seek medical care if symptoms worsen after day 5
Hospitalization for pneumonia complications
